analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: HyTEC literature review and dose-response modeling of spinal cord tolerance to **1-5 fraction SBRT (>6 Gy/fx)**. Peer-reviewed series 2005-2018: **40 screened, 7 de novo and 5 reirradiation** papers met inclusion. LQ with α/β 2 Gy used for conversions.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Series needed dosimetry at **spinal cord levels, not cauda equina**, an explicitly defined dose-reporting structure, and de novo vs reirradiation reported separately. Each series needed ≥3 pts and a reported follow-up.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Radiation myelopathy**, a diagnosis of exclusion. Most included cases were high grade (≥3) on CTCAE or RTOG/EORTC scales, since low-grade RM is masked by painful spinal mets.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Limits mostly refer to the **thecal sac**, used as a cord PRV (about 1.5 mm beyond cord in the thoracic spine, 2-3 mm in the upper cervical spine). The **14 Gy single-fraction** figure came from a **CT-myelogram cord** with the MSKCC technique.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Reirradiation: **cumulative thecal sac EQD2 Dmax ≤70 Gy**, SBRT EQD2 Dmax ≤25 Gy, ratio ≤0.5, interval ≥5 mo. Katsoulakis reported 2-yr cumulative RM incidence of **0.8%** after single-fraction 18-24 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Updates the **AAPM TG101** recommendations with data published since. At 14.6 Gy in 1 fx, the Sahgal 2013, QUANTEC and Gibbs models predict ~17%, ~8% and ~3% RM. The authors attribute Sahgal's high estimate partly to its small control cohort.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents de novo or reirradiation spine SBRT in 1-5 fractions at spinal cord levels. Does not represent the cauda equina or conventionally fractionated RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The largest complete cohort (228 pts) had only 2 RM events. Point Dmax carries high dose uncertainty, and both of those RM cases fell below the series median Dmax. Ten events would need **about 500 to 2000 pts**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The 1-5% band is a **risk label on existing constraints**, not a new constraint set. The authors call the 2-5 fraction LQ extrapolations unsupported and ask future series to report **D0.03cc** alongside Dmax.

studies.interpretation:
The report's most useful feature is that it declines to invent new limits. It takes the constraints already in circulation, mainly the Sahgal 2013 thecal sac values and the 14 Gy single-fraction cord figure from the MSKCC myelogram experience, and puts a modeled risk on them. A reader who wants 'the HyTEC number' should see it that way: the familiar 1 to 5 fraction ladder now carries an estimated 1-5% myelopathy risk, which is a consent figure, not proof that doses below it are safe. Compared with AAPM TG101, which reported doses to the spinal cord itself, the update moves the default reporting structure toward the thecal sac as a de facto PRV. That change matters as much as any number in the table.

The evidence underneath is thin, and the authors say so. Twelve series met inclusion, reported against three different structures. The Sahgal model was fitted on 9 grade 4 cases against 66 controls. That design pushes the curve toward conservatism, and one event at a thecal sac Dmax of 10.6 Gy may have pulled it further. The Ryu cross-check shows how far apart the models are. At 14.6 Gy in one fraction, Sahgal, QUANTEC and Gibbs predict roughly 17%, 8% and 3%. That spread, not the headline 1-5%, is the real uncertainty band a few Gy above the recommended limit. The KG model's interval at 14 Gy is tight, 0.5%-1.8%, but it reaches 5% only 2 Gy higher. That is why the authors quote a range instead of a point estimate.

The Katsoulakis cohort carries the most interesting signal and the least statistical power. It is the closest thing to a complete institutional denominator. Both myelopathy cases had a cord Dmax of 13.4 and 13.6 Gy, below the series median. So point Dmax may not be the variable that separates injured from uninjured cords. The V7Gy split (1 of 13 vs 1 of 246) suggests a low-dose volume effect, but two events cannot carry a constraint. The RTOG 0915 V7Gy limit tested in the same data neither predicted RM nor was met by most treatments, so lung SBRT constraints should not be carried over to the spine. The push to report D0.03cc alongside Dmax is the most practical forward-looking recommendation in the paper.

The 2-5 fraction values deserve more caution than the single-fraction figure. They depend on LQ conversion at α/β 2 in a dose-per-fraction range where the authors themselves question LQ validity. The straight conversions of 14 Gy are explicitly flagged as unusable in practice. The Sahgal multi-fraction column is the defensible option because it is conservative, not because it was observed.

For reirradiation, the four Sahgal 2012 rules rest on small cohorts with short follow-up. Median latency after reirradiation is 6 months, so a short series can miss late events. The paper would be wrong in the dangerous direction if complete cohorts showed RM at thecal sac doses inside these limits, especially with modern MRI-fused cord contouring and no PRV. The authors estimate that settling this needs registries of about 500 to 2000 pts.

open_questions: Is D0.03cc a more reliable RM predictor than point Dmax?
Clinically validated 2-5 fraction cord limits beyond LQ extrapolation
Safe cord dose for repeat SBRT after prior SBRT

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: HyTEC review of **published literature** (PubMed) on hypofractionated SBRT, usually **1-5 fractions**. **Logistic TCP models** fit by maximum likelihood to pooled reported outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Reported series spanning **preoperative (neoadjuvant), borderline resectable, and locally advanced** pancreatic cancer. The source does not give pt-level eligibility or N.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Fractionation differences handled with the **LQ model, α/β=10 Gy**, all doses expressed as **3-fraction equivalents**. Alliance A021501's **33 Gy/5 fx = 28.2 Gy/3 fx**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **1-year local control**, modeled separately **without surgery** and with **margin-negative resection**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: A **dose response across 25 to 36 Gy** 3-fx equivalents; the dose-by-LC grid is in the table above.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Places the **Alliance A021501** 33 Gy/5 fx regimen at **77% modeled 1-yr LC** without surgery, below the 30-36 Gy equivalent band. No randomized dose comparison exists in the source to test this.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localized pancreatic cancer treated with 1-5 fx SBRT, without surgery or after margin-negative resection. Does not represent conventionally fractionated chemoRT or metastatic disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **1-yr LC is a short horizon** in a disease where distant failure often comes first. The source abstract gives **no toxicity data** and does not state how LC was defined across pooled reports.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The value is a **common dose currency** for placing any pancreatic SBRT schedule on one curve. Whether the dose response survives adjustment for case mix, and whether **escalation is deliverable next to duodenum and stomach**, stays open.

studies.interpretation:
The useful output here is not a new efficacy estimate but a common dose currency. Pancreatic SBRT has been reported across 1 to 5 fractions with little agreement on schedule, and converting every regimen to a 3-fraction equivalent with α/β=10 Gy lets a reader place any schedule on one curve. On that curve the pooled data show a dose response in the 25 to 36 Gy range, 1-year LC without surgery of ≈79% to 86% at 30 to 36 Gy equivalents, and a fall below 70% under 24 Gy. The practical consequence is where the widely used 33 Gy in 5 fractions lands: 28.2 Gy in 3 fractions, with a modeled 77% 1-year LC, on the rising part of the curve rather than its plateau.

How much confidence that deserves depends on three modeling choices. First, the LQ framework and an α/β of 10 Gy are assumptions at ablative doses per fraction. The conversion is what makes the comparison possible, and it is also untested by the pooled data, so the position of any regimen on the curve inherits that uncertainty. Second, the inputs are published series, not pt-level data, so differences in selection, systemic therapy, response imaging and LC definitions across reports are absorbed into the fit rather than adjusted for. A dose response across institutions can partly reflect which centers treated to higher doses, and whom they treated. Third, 1-year LC is an early endpoint in a disease where distant progression and death often come first, which narrows the window in which a local control difference can show.

The resection finding needs its own reading. Above a 28 Gy 3-fraction equivalent, margin-negative resection carried 1-year LC above 90%. That is a selected group: pts who reach R0 surgery differ from those who do not in biology, response to systemic therapy and performance status. The figure describes a favorable subset, not an effect of dose plus surgery that a reader can apply to an individual pt.

Against the field, the result fits the direction of interest in dose escalation for pancreatic SBRT, and it gives the A021501 schedule a modeled local control estimate that can be weighed against escalation. What it does not settle is the cost. The source abstract reports no toxicity data, and the duodenum and stomach sit against most pancreatic targets, so a dose that reaches the plateau may not be deliverable in many anatomies. Nor does it connect local control to survival.

For the conclusion to be wrong, the apparent dose response would need to come mostly from case mix and institutional practice rather than dose, and literature-level pooling cannot exclude that. The authors' own call for caution is the right register. This is a hypothesis about where to aim, best tested in prospective dose-escalation studies with harmonized LC definitions and paired toxicity reporting.

That frames escalation beyond 33/5 as a testable LC question when GI organ-at-risk constraints allow it.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: HyTEC literature pooling with logistic NTCP modeling: **238** major vessel Dmax values from **6** articles (PubMed, April 2018). Two later dose-volume datasets (Mavroidis 2018 recalculation of Yazici 2013; Gebhardt 2018/Ling 2019) were modeled separately.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: H&N SBRT reirradiation after a prior course assumed at a nominal **70 Gy** conventional; prior dose was not reported per pt. Interval ranged **2 to 423 months**, median about 2 years, so guidance is framed for roughly a **≥6-month** interval.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Models use the **5-fraction** SBRT dose only, prior EBRT excluded. Gebhardt: median **44 Gy (40-50 Gy) in 5 fx, every other day**, with 1 to 3 courses summed as physical dose without a repair factor.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Grade 3 to 5 bleeding per CTCAE v4.0. **CBS** = carotid bleeding without adjacent persistent or progressive tumor; **BE** = any bleeding event, possibly tumor-driven. All but 1 dataset carry some BE.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Pooled Dmax model **TD50 45.7 Gy** (95% CI 39.6-64.9). Only **1 BE below Dmax 30 Gy**. With risk reduction (Gebhardt), modeled CBS **2.2%** at 1 cm3 >20 Gy and **<1%** at 0.1 cm3 >20 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Many cooperative group trials did not constrain carotid dose, and a systematic review put vessel injury risk at **1.3% to 4.5%**. RTOG 3507's carotid limits (**Dmax ≤42 Gy, D50% ≤32 Gy**) are nonvalidated and sit below the pooled Dmax TD50.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents recurrent H&N re-irradiated with 5-fx SBRT after a prior conventional course, with a roughly 6-month or longer interval. Does not represent de novo SBRT, a planned SBRT boost, or pts with longer life expectancy than the short-f/u series captured.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Vessel delineation varied (cephalad/caudad extent, branches), so only **D0.1cc/Dmax** compare across studies. Grouped cohort values (e.g. **87** non-BE pts nominally at a 20 Gy limit) stand in for per-pt data. Summed SBRT courses ignore repair.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Lower toxicity in the risk-reduction series suggests the strategies work, but they were applied together, so **each factor's weight is unknown**. Missing a carotid constraint should not by itself preclude retreatment, since recurrent H&N pts are **4 to 5 times** more likely to die of uncontrolled disease than of a modern reirradiation complication.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this report is less the curves than the constraint they imply. The pooled Dmax model places the 50% tolerance dose at 45.7 Gy in 5 fractions, but it is built from 238 vessel points of which large blocks are grouped cohort values (87 non-bleeding cases sitting nominally at a 20 Gy limit, 60 at a median of 34.7 Gy). The low-risk tail, which is where a planner actually works, therefore rests on few individually measured events. The authors' own reading, that Dmax below 20 to 30 Gy appears associated with low risk, is the defensible takeaway. The TD50 itself is not something to plan against.

The more informative comparison is internal. The Gebhardt series, treated every other day with risk-reduction strategies applied, yielded modeled grade 3 to 5 CBS of 2.2% with 1 cm3 above 20 Gy and under 1% at 0.1 cm3, even though its cumulative SBRT doses run well above those on the pooled x-axis. That fits the idea that alternating-day delivery and patient selection matter at least as much as dose. But the series bundled every strategy together, so it cannot say which one carried the effect, and its model rests on 5 events in 4 pts. Endpoint definitions also diverge: Gebhardt scored CBS without adjacent tumor, while the pooled data include bleeding that may be tumor-driven, which biases the older curves toward higher apparent vessel toxicity.

For practice, the backdrop is that many cooperative group trials historically left the carotid unconstrained. RTOG 3507 carries carotid limits of Dmax ≤42 Gy and D50% ≤32 Gy, which the authors present as nonvalidated but conservative next to these data. Read them as planning targets rather than hard stops. The paper is explicit that missing them should not preclude retreatment, given that recurrent H&N pts are 4 to 5 times more likely to die of uncontrolled disease than of a modern reirradiation complication.

Two methodological choices should temper confidence. First, the prior course was never summed. A nominal 70 Gy was assumed and left out of every model, and the interval ranged from 2 to 423 months, so the curves describe reirradiation dose alone in a population whose cumulative carotid exposure varied widely. Second, vessel delineation was inconsistent across studies, which is why the authors limit cross-study comparison to D0.1cc and Dmax. A D50% constraint like RTOG 3507's depends on how much carotid was contoured, so it does not transfer cleanly between institutions.

The paper does not settle whether proactive stenting or conventional/hyperfractionated retreatment is the better path for circumferential involvement. It also does not show whether these thresholds hold in longer survivors, since median follow-up was under 2 years in nearly every series. It reads as a plea for per-patient composite-dose reporting as much as a set of constraints.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Small-volume carotid dose above 20 Gy is the planning lever: with alternating-day delivery and risk-reduction strategies, modeled G3-5 CBS was 2.2% at 1 cm3 >20 Gy and <1% at 0.1 cm3 in 5 fx. RTOG 3507's Dmax ≤42 Gy and D50% ≤32 Gy are reasonable targets, not hard stops.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Practical contouring guideline with radio-anatomy of V1, V2 and V3 pathways, imaging review and illustrative cases (palate ACC, masticator rhabdomyosarcoma, recurrent parotid ACC). **No outcome series of its own.**

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion

analysis_sections.body: **CTV-P1 = GTV + 5 mm** along the nerve (primary RT) or **positive margin + 5 mm** (R1 post-op). **CTV-P2 = nerve path ≥30 mm**, skull base extension discussed and often recommended, to brainstem if skull base involved; bilateral paths for non-lateralized tumors.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Zukauskaite's 1576-pt primary RT SCC series placed most recurrences in the GTV, but **excluded ACC, nasopharynx, paranasal sinus and skin**, the settings this guideline targets. EORTC 22931 informs adding cisplatin, not the volume.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents H&N SCC with extensive PNI, ACC, and tumors invading the PPF, masticator space, nasopharynx or maxillary sinus treated with IMRT. Does not represent focal microscopic PNI without other risk features, where adjuvant RT is case-by-case.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The **focal vs extensive PNI** threshold drives very different volumes but is not standardized in source. Particle RT for inoperable or residual ACC is suggested **despite the lack of randomized evidence**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The argument rests on imaging underestimating continuous nerve spread, so the enhancement edge is treated as a lower bound. The guideline does not settle whether tighter nerve volumes would produce marginal failures.

studies.interpretation:
This is an anatomy-first contouring guideline, and its value rests on one argument: perineural spread is a continuous pathologic process that imaging samples incompletely, so the elective target has to follow the nerve rather than the enhancement. Two numbers carry the recommendation, a 5 mm expansion along the nerve path for the high-risk volume and an extension of at least 30 mm for the low-risk volume, with coverage to the skull base discussed and often favored. Neither comes from an outcome series in the source. Both are expert positions built on radio-anatomy and on the documented failure modes of MRI.

That imaging evidence is the strongest part of the paper. MRI is described as highly sensitive for macroscopic PNI, yet the surgical correlation series it cites show MRI misjudging extent in 5 of 30 and in 4 of 36 detected cases, and missing disease outright in 2 of 38. Add radiologic skip lesions over disease that is usually continuous on pathology, and the enhancement edge becomes a lower bound. The 30 mm figure is best read as a reasonable response to a known underestimation bias, not as a measured distance of microscopic spread.

Against the outcome data the source does cite, the guideline pulls in a different direction from the Zukauskaite primary RT series of 1576 pts, in which most recurrences sat within the GTV. The authors handle this fairly: that series was SCC only and excluded nasopharynx, paranasal sinus and skin, precisely the sites and histologies where nerve spread dominates. An in-GTV failure pattern therefore does not refute elective nerve-path coverage for ACC or PPF-invading disease; it simply was not tested there. EORTC 22931 enrolled pts with PNI and supports concurrent cisplatin for locoregional control, but it speaks to the systemic add-on, not to how far along the nerve to draw.

The guideline is weakest at the boundary between focal and extensive microscopic PNI. Focal PNI without other high-risk features is a relative, case-by-case adjuvant indication with a low-risk volume confined to nerve paths in the tumor bed, while extensive PNI earns the full 30 mm path. That threshold depends on the pathology report and is not defined in the source, so two centers reading similar specimens could contour very different volumes. Skull base extension also forces trade-offs against brainstem and optic pathway that are left to individual judgment, which is honest but offers no dose-constraint guidance.

What would make it wrong is a patterns-of-failure series in ACC or sinonasal disease showing nerve-path recurrences beyond the recommended extension, or, in the other direction, no marginal failures with tighter volumes. Until such data exist, the practical contribution is the map itself: the PPF as a hub, the V1 to V2 communication at the orbital apex, and the three V-VII junctions are the structures most easily omitted when contouring on axial CT alone.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: MRI misdefined PNI extent in 5 of 30 and 4 of 36 operated cases, with skip lesions over continuous disease, so the enhancement edge understates spread. That justifies a ≥30 mm nerve-path CTV-P2 with V-VII junctions and the PPF hub included, rather than enhancement plus 5 mm alone.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Consensus guideline from an expert panel representing **DAHANCA, EORTC, HKNPCSG, NCIC CTG, NCRI, RTOG and TROG**: radiation oncologists, a head and neck surgeon and an anatomist. No voting or agreement metrics are reported in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Defines **CT boundaries for nodal CTV delineation** for levels Ia through Xb on axial CT, with the pt in **neutral position**. A 110-slice DICOM-RT atlas was distributed for teaching.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Extends the **Robbins-modified levels** and maps them against the **TNM atlas** groups for neck nodes. It adds named levels for the retropharyngeal, retro-styloid, parotid, bucco-facial and posterior skull groups, and moves the level V cranial limit to the hyoid bone.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents nodal CTV delineation for node-negative, node-positive and post-operative head and neck RT on axial CT in neutral position. Does not represent the choice of which levels to treat or the dose levels, which the panel left out of scope.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Some boundaries are **set arbitrarily** (the IVa caudal limit) rather than derived from anatomy or failure patterns. The landmarks need adapting for **hyperextended positioning**, especially near the skull base, and the inconstant medial retropharyngeal group is **not covered**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The value is consistency: common boundaries across cooperative groups reduce variation between pts and institutions and make multi-institutional trial contours comparable. It tells you where a level ends, not whether to include it.

studies.interpretation:
This document is best read as shared infrastructure, not evidence. It makes no claim about control or toxicity. What it does is give every cooperative group running head and neck RT trials the same anatomic vocabulary, so a trial protocol that says level IVa or level VIIa means the same volume in Copenhagen, Hong Kong and Toronto. That is the main thing it changes. Trial results on elective nodal coverage only transfer between centers if the levels are drawn the same way, and before a common atlas, two contours both labeled level V could differ substantially at the cranial end.

The structural choices deserve a closer look. Adopting the Robbins framework, a surgical nomenclature, keeps the RT contour aligned with the levels a surgeon reports on a neck dissection specimen. That makes pathology-driven post-op CTVs easier to translate. The trade-off is that some limits inherit surgical convention rather than lymphatic anatomy. The IVa caudal limit was set by reference to how far a dissection usually reaches, and the panel says outright that it is arbitrary. Moving the level V cranial limit to the hyoid is the reverse trade, an imaging landmark replacing a soft-tissue one, and it reassigns the uppermost posterior nodes to the occipital group. Both choices favor reproducibility on CT over anatomic purity, which suits a contouring guideline.

The expansion beyond the classic levels matters most for primaries that drain atypically: skin cancers of the scalp, face and auricle, parotid tumors, nasopharynx with retro-styloid spread, and lower lip or anterior floor of mouth lesions draining to the upper VIb nodes. Here the guideline lets a reader name and draw a volume that older atlases left to individual judgment. The VIb rule is a good example. The cranial limit sits at the thyroid cartilage by default but rises to the hyoid only for the primaries that feed the inconstant infrahyoid nodes, a site-conditional boundary built into the atlas itself.

The main limitation is what the panel excluded. The guideline deliberately leaves out which levels to treat for a given primary and N stage, and at what dose, so it cannot by itself support omitting or adding a level. The panel's own descriptions of which primaries put each level at risk are drainage statements, not validated risk thresholds. The landmarks also assume neutral positioning, and the panel admits that hyperextension changes level relationships near the skull base. Centers that hyperextend routinely need their own adaptation.

No agreement statistics, inter-observer data or failure-pattern validation are reported, so confidence here rests on panel composition, not measurement. For a radiation oncologist, the practical stance is to use it as the default boundary reference and pair it with a separate, evidence-based decision on level selection, rather than reading the atlas as an endorsement of any particular elective volume.

VIb starts at the thyroid cartilage except for anterior FOM, tongue tip and lower lip primaries. Only lateral retropharyngeal nodes count as VIIa, which sets how far medially the CTV reaches.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review by four European radiation oncologists, **Oral Oncology 2018**, summarizing the international nodal-level guidelines (updated 2013) and the international primary-tumor CTV consensus. Recommendations are **expert opinion**, not trial-derived.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Primary RT for **oral cavity, oropharyngeal, hypopharyngeal and laryngeal SCC**, nodal staging per **AJCC/UICC 8th ed**. Valid for p16-negative and p16-positive OPC; **not valid postoperatively or for adenoid cystic carcinoma**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Selective neck RT for **N0-N1** (oral cavity I-III; pharynx/larynx II-IVa), **Ib-V for N2a/N2b/N3**. Primary **CTV-P2 = GTV + 10 mm** with anatomic editing; nodal therapeutic CTV = **nodal GTV + 5 mm**. SIB: **54-56 Gy** prophylactic, **70 Gy in 33-35 fx** therapeutic.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Positions the international consensus between the **anatomic compartment approach** (French school, larger volumes, 2-3 cm where no barrier) and the **DAHANCA geometric approach** (GTV + 5 mm, + 5 mm). Authors expect consensus volumes to be smaller than anatomic in all directions and smaller than DAHANCA mainly axially for T1-T2.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents definitive IMRT for oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx and larynx SCC. Does not represent the postoperative neck, adenoid cystic carcinoma, or nasopharynx.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: No systematic volumetric comparison of the three approaches; the worked examples are single cases. Whether margin reduction raises **geographic miss** is stated as an ongoing DAHANCA analysis, so the safety of the tighter primary CTV is not yet demonstrated.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for tight primary margins rests on two observations: pathology showing infiltration typically within **5 mm** of gross tumor, and recurrence mapping showing failures **mainly within the GTV**. Both point to **dose and biology, not margin**, as the lever for local control.

studies.interpretation:
The central argument of this review is that head and neck target definition has converged on a probabilistic compromise: cover enough tissue that local failures at the CTV edge stay rare, and no more, because every additional millimetre of mucosa, constrictor and gland costs toxicity that IMRT was supposed to spare. The authors frame target-volume heterogeneity as a source of variation large enough to erase the IMRT gain, which is a reasonable premise, but the review itself offers no outcome data showing that adopting these guidelines improves control or toxicity. The concluding claim that the guidelines will improve outcome is an expectation, not a finding.

On the neck, the recommendations are the familiar selective-treatment logic built on predictable drainage in an undisturbed neck. The parts worth a reader's attention are the exceptions. N1 hypopharynx is carved out of the selective template because of its propensity for nodal spread, and lateralized oral cavity tumors with N2a or more are flagged for contralateral treatment on the basis of reported contralateral involvement with multiple ipsilateral nodes. The p16-positive oropharynx statement is the weakest link: the authors say there is no data to support different level selection, which is an absence of evidence, and the TNM 8th edition restaging means N categories no longer carry the same nodal burden they did when the selective-neck data were generated. The advice to weigh node number, location and laterality rather than the N label is the practical response.

On the primary, the review sets out three schools. The anatomic compartment approach treats whole compartments once a barrier is breached and falls back on 2-3 cm margins where no barrier exists, which the authors expect to produce the largest volumes. DAHANCA's geometric approach assumes tumor density falls with distance and uses a 5 mm plus 5 mm structure; its documented benefit is inter-center consistency, not proven control. The international consensus takes the geometric expansion and adds anatomic editing, which inherits the reproducibility argument while letting barriers trim the volume.

The evidence that a tight high-dose margin is safe comes from two places, and both deserve scrutiny. Pathology series showing infiltration largely within 5 mm are drawn from resected, mostly smaller tumors, which may not represent the bulky T3-T4 disease that dominates definitive RT practice. The Danish three-center comparison, where margins ranged from 0 to 10 mm and local relapse tracked neither, is retrospective and confounded by whatever else differed between centers. The observation that out-of-CTV failures still sat inside the 95% isodose is useful: it suggests that dose fall-off, not contour edges, protected those patients, which argues that a highly conformal plan would be less forgiving.

What would make the framework wrong is a rise in marginal failures once tighter, edited CTVs are delivered with steeper gradients. The authors acknowledge that analysis is ongoing within DAHANCA. Until those data exist, the guidelines are best read as a reproducibility standard with a plausible safety rationale, and the authors' own caveat that missing endoscopy or degraded imaging should push the clinician toward a larger GTV is the right default.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The trade is explicit: N1 hypopharynx is pulled out of the selective II-IVa template, and oral cavity N2a+ is flagged for contralateral coverage even when lateralized. On the primary, a Danish 3-center series found local relapse unrelated to margin across 0 to 10 mm, which supports a GTV + 5 mm high-dose CTV.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International **multi-society consensus guideline** for primary-tumour CTV (CTV-P) delineation in laryngeal, hypopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and oral cavity SCC, illustrated with endoscopy-matched planning CT cases by subsite and T stage.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **CTV-P1 = GTV-P + 5 mm** for the high dose (typically 70 Gy in 2 Gy fractions over 7 weeks); **CTV-P2 = GTV-P + 10 mm** for the prophylactic (typically 50 Gy) or intermediate (typically 60 Gy) dose. Every expansion is edited for air, abutting subsites and strong barriers such as bone and fascia unless invaded.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Margins rest on resection-specimen infiltration data and transoral series: laser surgery with a 2-3 mm mucosal margin gives **LC 85-95%** in T1-T2 larynx, and tonsil T1-T2 with at least 2-3 mm gives **LC above 90%**, both without PORT.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents definitive (primary-setting) RT for laryngeal, hypopharyngeal, oropharyngeal and oral cavity SCC. Does not represent post-operative or recurrent disease, where anatomy is perturbed by prior treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Supporting surgical series were **highly selected and mostly HPV-positive**, and the effect of HPV on required margin is unknown. Infiltrative borders and tumour budding challenge the decreasing-density assumption, and **subglottic SCC (<5% of laryngeal SCC)** rules rest on very few data.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document standardizes nomenclature (CTV-P1/P2/P3) independently of dose-level count, which matters for multicentre trials and peer review. PTV expansion is explicitly left to each centre, so the guideline fixes the clinical volume, not the delivered one.

studies.interpretation:
The core move here is to replace subsite-by-subsite institutional habit with one geometric rule, a 5 mm expansion for the high-dose volume and a 10 mm expansion for the lower-dose volume, and then to spend most of the document on how that rule must be bent by anatomy. That ordering is the right one. A pure isotropic margin in the larynx or pharynx will cross air, cartilage, bone and fascia that tumour cells do not freely traverse, and the guideline's insistence that the expansion is a starting point to be edited, not a finished volume, is what makes it usable across subsites as different as a T1 vocal cord and a T4 piriform sinus.

The evidentiary base deserves a careful read. The margins are anchored in two kinds of data: pathology specimens showing how far tumour infiltrates beyond the gross edge, and transoral surgical series where small primaries controlled with 2-3 mm margins achieved local control in the 85-95% range for larynx and above 90% for tonsil without post-operative RT. Both support the claim that microscopic disease is concentrated close to the GTV. Neither is a test of the RT margin itself. Surgical series were selected by experienced surgeons with direct visualization of mucosal extent, and the oropharyngeal cohorts were mostly HPV-positive. The authors say as much. What follows is that the 5 mm high-dose margin is better supported for small, well-defined primaries than for infiltrative ones, and the document flags infiltrative borders and tumour budding as precisely the scenario where GTV definition and therefore the whole construct becomes less reliable.

The hypopharyngeal carve-out is the most clinically consequential departure. Reported submucosal spread up to 20-30 mm cranio-caudal is the reason the guideline offers a 15 mm cranio-caudal margin to CTV-P2 there. A centre that applies the default 10 mm everywhere would systematically under-cover the direction in which hypopharyngeal disease is most likely to travel. Conversely, the explicit statement that T1 glottic disease needs no CTV-P2 supports small-volume larynx-only treatment, consistent with how early glottic cancer is already commonly treated.

Two boundaries limit transfer. First, the guideline is for the primary setting only; post-operative and recurrent disease are excluded because prior treatment perturbs the anatomy the editing rules depend on. Second, it defines the CTV, not the PTV, and leaves set-up and motion margins to each centre's immobilization and imaging. Two departments can therefore adopt these CTVs faithfully and still treat materially different volumes.

What would make the framework wrong is a pattern of marginal failures concentrated just outside CTV-P1 in edited regions, particularly where cartilage or fascia was assumed to be a barrier. That is a testable question in prospective patterns-of-failure work, and it is the evidence this consensus, by design, does not supply.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM HyTEC **systematic literature review with logistic TCP modeling**: 24 PubMed-indexed articles, **2619 spinal metastases**, 30 dose/fractionation data points. Maximum-likelihood fits with profile-likelihood CIs. Studies were down-weighted where their patients overlapped.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Spinal metastases treated with SBRT in **1 to 5 fractions**. Studies of primary spinal tumors and of spinal cord or dural tumors were excluded. Previously irradiated and unirradiated metastases were **pooled** when not reported separately, and histology was not stratified.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Separate physical-dose models for 1, 4 and 5 fx. Data for 2 and 3 fx were too sparse to model separately, so all fractionations were pooled in **3-fraction equivalent dose with α/β 6 Gy**. CTV conventionally includes the adjacent vertebral segments, with a PTV margin of 0 to 2 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Actuarial 2-year local tumor control** as each source article defined it. SPINO criteria are cited for local progression, and pseudoprogression was reported in 18% of spine SBRT treatments.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **90% TCP at 20 Gy/1 fx, 28 Gy/2 fx, 33 Gy/3 fx and 40 Gy/5 fx (extrapolated)**. The most common schemes give model 2y LC of **82% to 96%**. Per-regimen estimates are in the tables above.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: SC24 and RTOG 0631 are the randomized spinal SBRT trials, and they compare SBRT with conventional RT for pain response. This analysis does something different: it estimates the dose-control relationship across SBRT regimens, which neither trial was designed to test.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents spinal metastases treated with 1 to 5 fx SBRT, previously irradiated or not, across histologies. Does not represent postoperative SBRT (not addressed), primary spinal tumors, or histology-specific dosing.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The series span **2006 to 2018**, so changes in image guidance and target definition are folded into the curve. Tumor volume was not modeled. The narrow 95% CIs sit against widely scattered data, which the authors read as **unmodeled variance**, not precision.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: With no standard spinal SBRT prescription, the curves support **18 to 24 Gy/1 fx, 24 Gy/2 fx and 27 to 30 Gy/3 fx** as the clinically accepted range. Higher-dose regimens raise estimated TCP, and that gain has to be weighed against toxicity. The epidural minimum dose, not the named prescription, is the parameter most likely to move control.

studies.interpretation:
The value here is a dose-response curve for a field that has never agreed on a prescription. Spinal SBRT ranges from 16 Gy to 24 Gy in a single fraction and spreads across 2, 3, 4 and 5 fraction schedules, and before this analysis no shared estimate linked those choices to local control. The curve is steep where practice sits: the composite model moves from 72% at 16 Gy to 96% at 24 Gy in one fraction. If the shape is roughly right, choosing a dose within the accepted range changes expected control by a margin a radiation oncologist would care about.

The x-axis is the weak point. Each data point uses the stated prescription dose, because almost no source article reported target coverage or minimum dose. Spinal SBRT plans routinely undercover the epidural margin to keep the cord maximum within 10 to 14 Gy in one fraction, and that margin is where recurrences cluster. The model therefore relates control to a dose that much of the tumor never received. The cited 811-lesion series makes the point concretely: at an identical 24 Gy prescription, 2-year control separated sharply by PTV D95. For planning, coverage of the epidural interface is probably the lever, and the prescription is only a rough proxy for it.

The fractionation comparisons depend on the α/β of 6 Gy. The authors reached it by matching isoeffect levels between schedules, the individual comparisons ran from 3 to 12 Gy, and they call the averaging arbitrary. A reader weighing 24 Gy in 2 fractions against 27 Gy in 3 is relying on that conversion as much as on data, and the 4 and 5 fraction estimates at the high end are extrapolations. The model's apparent edge for single-fraction schemes should be held loosely. The authors cite a separate systematic review leaning the same way, which carries the same data-quality limits.

Several confounders point in a direction a skeptic would flag. Lower doses are more often given to previously irradiated tumors because of cord tolerance, and those tumors control less well, so dose and prior irradiation are entangled in the pooled curve. Actuarial control that censors at death likely overstates durability in a population whose systemic disease and local regrowth progress together. The pooled series also span more than a decade of improving image guidance. All three effects could steepen or inflate the curve.

SC24 and RTOG 0631 test whether SBRT beats conventional palliative RT on pain. This analysis assumes SBRT is already chosen and asks which SBRT dose to use. It does not settle single versus multifraction for the therapeutic ratio, and it does not address postoperative SBRT. Its most durable contribution may be the reporting standard it asks for: full dosimetry tied to control, and cumulative incidence with death as a competing risk.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: At a fixed 24 Gy/1 fx, 2y control was 98% with PTV D95 >22.4 Gy vs 85% with <16.5 Gy, so epidural coverage near the cord matters more than the named prescription. These curves help choose among 18 to 24 Gy/1 fx, 24 Gy/2 fx and 27 to 30 Gy/3 fx, but the multifraction comparisons rest on an assumed α/β of 6 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: AAPM WGSBRT **HyTEC pooled analysis**: logistic dose-response models fit to study-level data from **56 of 2951** screened PubMed manuscripts (1995 to Sep 2017), **13,929 brain mets**. No individual-patient data.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Studies with **≥10 pts per dose/fractionation/size stratum** and ≥1-yr actuarial LC. Size by RTOG 90-05: **≤20 mm small, 21-30 mm medium, 31-40 mm large**. Most common primaries lung, melanoma, RCC, breast; most pts RPA class II.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Median prescription **20 Gy x1** (range 13-32 Gy in 1-5 fx), dose to PTV margin. Median GTV-PTV margin **1 mm** (0-3 mm). Half GK, the rest LINAC, robotic or tomotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** local control per metastasis, most often >20% diameter increase vs pre-SRS. OS per pt from SRS where reported.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Size-by-dose LC in the table above. Fractionation benefit clearest for **2-yr LC of large tumors** (P = .0014). Melanoma had the steepest curve, with **90% LC at 23.4 Gy** single fraction.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 90-05 fixed the 24/18/15 Gy size-based MTDs on toxicity in re-irradiated pts, with in-field control ≈50% and 2-yr necrosis 11%. HyTEC shows those MTDs buy **75% and ~69% LC** for medium and large lesions, and extends the earlier Wiggenraad pooled model, which used 12 data points from 11 papers.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intact brain mets in adults treated with SRS or fSRS alone. Does not represent postoperative cavities, SRS with concurrent systemic therapy, pediatric pts, or re-irradiation after WBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: 99% of small-tumor data were single fraction, so **α/β was fit on medium-large tumors only**. Histology not stratified except melanoma (4 studies, all small, all single fraction). Literature closes Sep 2017, before broad IO and CNS-penetrant targeted therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data support **de-escalating to ~18 Gy** for small non-melanoma mets and **fractionating lesions >20 mm** with regimens such as 30 Gy/3 or 35 Gy/5. The high α/β that powers the fractionation case may partly encode era and selection differences between fractionated and single-fraction series.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this analysis is calibration rather than discovery. RTOG 90-05 set the single-fraction doses the field still uses, 24, 18 and 15 Gy by diameter, but it set them on toxicity in previously irradiated pts, and tumor control was never its endpoint; its in-field control estimate sat around 50%. HyTEC asks the inverse question: given the doses practice adopted, what local control do they actually buy at each size? The answer sorts cleanly into two decisions. For small lesions, 18 Gy already lands above 85% at 1 year, which argues against reflexively pushing a non-melanoma lesion ≤20 mm to the 24 Gy ceiling. For medium and large lesions, the 90-05 MTDs deliver 75% and ~69%, a ceiling imposed by necrosis risk rather than by any efficacy plateau, and that is the opening for fractionation.

The fractionation case rests almost entirely on α/β. The fit here implies roughly 22 Gy, and the authors adopt 20 Gy, far above the 10 Gy conventionally assumed for tumor. If that is right, 3- and 5-fraction schedules deliver more tumor-effective dose than 20 Gy/1 while sparing normal brain, which is the best of both directions. A skeptic should hold that number loosely. It was estimated from medium-to-large tumors only, because nearly all small-tumor data were single fraction, and from study-level points where fractionated series differ from single-fraction series in era, platform, margin and selection. A high α/β fitted across institutions can absorb those differences and present them as radiobiology. The 2-yr large-tumor signal is the most persuasive piece, but it rests on 8 fractionated data points.

The OS observation is the tell for confounding. Fractionated points more often exceeded 50% 1-yr OS, and the higher-survival points clustered in recent publications, which places fractionated series disproportionately in the modern systemic era. The direction of the resulting LC bias is not obvious: actuarial censoring at death overstates control most where death is common, which plausibly flatters older single-fraction series and would narrow, not widen, the apparent fractionation benefit. Pseudoprogression scored as failure pushes the other way. Neither can be untangled without per-lesion data.

The melanoma curve, rising from 19.5% at 18 Gy to 95% at 24.6 Gy, is the steepest relationship reported, but it comes from four single-fraction small-tumor studies. Treat it as a directional argument for dose in melanoma rather than a calibrated curve, and recognize that IO-era pseudoprogression in melanoma makes MRI-defined failure especially unreliable.

What the analysis cannot settle is exactly where practice has since moved: postoperative cavities, SRS delivered alongside IO or CNS-penetrant targeted therapy, cumulative dose after prior WBRT, and histology-specific dosing beyond melanoma. The authors state that no randomized trial has compared local control across SRS and fSRS schedules. Until one does, these curves are the best available dose reference for intact lesions, and their fractionation conclusion is a well-reasoned model inference rather than a tested result.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Large lesions carry the fractionation case: single-fraction 2-yr LC never cleared 60%, while 7 of 8 fractionated points did (P = .0014). At α/β 20 Gy, 30 Gy/3 and 35 Gy/5 give 8% and 11.5% more tumor SFED than 20 Gy/1, supporting fSRS over the RTOG 90-05 MTD above 20 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ESTRO ACROP committee guideline built from a **structured questionnaire, then consensus discussion and voting**. Each recommendation is graded **Mandatory, Recommended, Optional or Discouraged**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Primary CTV = GTV + **e.g. 5-8 mm**, edited to anatomic barriers. Nodal CTV is either the **whole involved station** or a **5-8 mm geometric expansion**. Elective nodal CTV beyond the hilum and neighbouring stations is **discouraged**. PTV follows ICRU, with motion handled by ITV, MidV/MidP or gating/tracking.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The guideline supports involved-field nodal volumes with **large multicentre trials** that used station-based CTVs without unacceptable out-of-field mediastinal recurrence, but the source excerpt names none of them. It also does not address consolidation immunotherapy after chemoRT (PACIFIC) as a planning consideration.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents locally advanced NSCLC treated with curative-intent conventionally fractionated or moderately hypofractionated RT or chemo-RT, including PORT by analogy. Does not represent SBRT for early-stage disease, where the OAR and volume rules here are not intended to apply.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Grades reflect committee agreement, not level of evidence**, and the excerpt reports no vote margins. Several Mandatory items, such as the pre-chemo nodal GTV, are expert positions rather than randomized findings.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The decisions with real effect are about nodes: **PET+ overrides a negative EBUS/EUS**, and elective nodal coverage needs a justification. Leaving station-based vs geometric nodal CTV open means different centres can treat different volumes while both following the guideline.

studies.interpretation:
This guideline matters most for its nodal rules, not its margin numbers. It resolves the common PET-positive, EBUS/EUS-negative node toward inclusion in the GTV, because endosonographic false-negative rates are high. Only a non-malignant biopsy explanation or a negative mediastinoscopy permits leaving such a node out. It also makes involved-field practice the default: elective nodal coverage beyond the hilum and adjacent stations is discouraged. A centre that treats the elective mediastinum now needs a reason to do it. A centre that trims volumes on one negative needle aspirate now needs stronger negative evidence.

The case for dropping elective nodal irradiation rests on a reference to large multicentre trials that used station-based nodal CTVs without unacceptable out-of-field mediastinal recurrence. The excerpt does not name those trials or say what threshold counted as unacceptable, so the reader has to accept that judgement on trust. The two nodal CTV options are presented as equivalent, but they are not the same volume. Covering the whole involved station is larger than a geometric expansion around the nodal GTV, especially for a small node at the edge of a station. That difference changes oesophageal and cardiac dose. The document addresses it only by noting that margins can be adjusted near neighbouring organs.

The method should temper how much weight each grade gets. The grades come from a questionnaire and a committee vote. The excerpt reports no vote margins, so a near-unanimous Mandatory item cannot be told apart from a narrowly carried one. Some Mandatory items are reasonable expert positions that have never been tested head to head. One example is keeping every pre-induction involved node in the GTV even after it is no longer visible. Their label reflects how strongly the committee agreed, not the quality of evidence behind them. Leaving motion management open (ITV, mid-ventilation or mid-position, gating or tracking) is defensible, since none of these approaches has shown better outcomes. The side effect is that volumes from centres that all follow this guideline are not directly comparable.

The document also reflects its time. It addresses conventionally fractionated or moderately hypofractionated RT with chemotherapy as the only systemic partner. It does not consider consolidation immunotherapy after chemoRT (PACIFIC), where lung and oesophageal exposure may interact with later systemic treatment. The heart is a mandatory OAR, but substructure contouring is only optional. A reader planning today may reasonably treat that as a minimum.

The guideline's recommendations could be undermined in several ways: station-based and geometric nodal CTVs could turn out to have different out-of-field nodal failure rates, or including PET-positive, EBUS-negative nodes could add toxicity without improving regional control. The authors name inter-observer variation as one of the main uncertainties in lung delineation. That suggests the quality-assurance recommendations (supervised contouring, departmental instructions, peer review) may do more for consistency between patients than any single margin choice in the document.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The nodal rules have the most effect on volumes. A PET+/EBUS-negative node stays in the GTV, every pre-chemo involved node stays in after induction, and elective nodal CTV beyond the hilum and adjacent stations is discouraged. The choice between whole-station and 5-8 mm geometric nodal CTV is left to the clinician, which affects oesophageal and cardiac dose.

papers.title: Modeling clinical outcomes in radiotherapy: NTCP, TCP and the “TECs”
papers.abstract: Abstract Radiation therapy is a double‐edged sword which damages both tumor and normal cells. Achieving treatments with high tumor control probability (TCP) yet low normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) is often a struggle because we rarely have a unified understanding of the dosimetric and clinical correlates of the desired outcomes. I am fortunate to have participated in some of these struggles, including analyzing and using in‐house data and being involved in the AAPM and ASTRO “TEC” projects—QUANTEC (Quantitatie Analysis of Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic), HyTEC (Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic) and PENTEC (Pediatric Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic).

papers.title: Comparison of Risks of Late Effects From Radiation Therapy in Children Versus Adults: Insights From the QUANTEC, HyTEC, and PENTEC Efforts
papers.abstract: Pediatric Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic (PENTEC) seeks to refine quantitative radiation dose-volume relationships for normal-tissue complication probabilities (NTCPs) in survivors of pediatric cancer. This article summarizes the evolution of PENTEC and compares it with similar adult-focused efforts (eg, Quantitative Analysis of Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic [QUANTEC] and Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic [HyTEC]) with respect to content, oversight, support, scope, and methodology of literature review. It then summarizes key organ-specific findings from PENTEC in an attempt to compare NTCP estimates in children versus adults. In brief, select normal-tissue risks within developing organs and tissues (eg, maldevelopment of musculoskeletal tissue, teeth, breasts, and reproductive organs) are primarily relevant only in children. For some organs and tissues, children appear to have similar (eg, brain for necrosis, optic apparatus, parotid gland, liver), greater (eg, brain for neurocognition, cerebrovascular, breast for lactation), less (ovary), or perhaps slightly less (eg, lung) risks of toxicity versus adults. Similarly, even within the broad pediatric age range (including adolescence), for some endpoints, younger children have greater (eg, hearing and brain for neurocognition) or lesser (eg, ovary, thyroid) risks of radiation-associated toxicities. NTCP comparisons in adults versus children are often confounded by marked differences in treatment paradigms that expose normal tissues to radiation (ie, cancer types, prescribed radiation therapy dose and fields, and chemotherapy agents used). To add to the complexity, it is unclear if age is best analyzed as a continuous variable versus with age groupings (eg, infants, young children, adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults, older adults). Further work is needed to better understand the complex manner in which age and developmental status affect risk.

papers.title: Biological Principles of Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT) and Stereotactic Radiation Surgery (SRS): Indirect Cell Death
papers.abstract: Purpose To review the radiobiological mechanisms of stereotactic body radiation therapy stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) and stereotactic radiation surgery (SRS). Methods and materials We reviewed previous reports and recent observations on the effects of high-dose irradiation on tumor cell survival, tumor vasculature, and antitumor immunity. We then assessed the potential implications of these biological changes associated with SBRT and SRS. Results Irradiation with doses higher than approximately 10 Gy/fraction causes significant vascular injury in tumors, leading to secondary tumor cell death. Irradiation of tumors with high doses has also been reported to increase the antitumor immunity, and various approaches are being investigated to further elevate antitumor immunity. The mechanism of normal tissue damage by high-dose irradiation needs to be further investigated. Conclusions In addition to directly killing tumor cells, high-dose irradiation used in SBRT and SRS induces indirect tumor cell death via vascular damage and antitumor immunity. Further studies are warranted to better understand the biological mechanisms underlying the high efficacy of clinical SBRT and SRS and to further improve the efficacy of SBRT and SRS.

papers.title: Initial Data Pooling for Radiation Dose-Volume Tolerance for Carotid Artery Blowout and Other Bleeding Events in Hypofractionated Head and Neck Retreatments
papers.abstract: Purpose Dose-volume data for injury to carotid artery and other major vessels in stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT)/SABR head and neck reirradiation were reviewed, modeled, and summarized. Methods and materials A PubMed search of the English-language literature (stereotactic and carotid and radiation) in April 2018 found 238 major vessel maximum point doses in 6 articles that were pooled for logistic modeling. Two subsequent studies with dose-volume major vessel data were modeled separately for comparison. Attempts were made to separate carotid blowout syndrome from other bleeding events (BE) in the analysis, but we acknowledge that all except 1 data set has some element of BE interspersed. Results Prior radiation therapy (RT) dose was not uniformly reported per patient in the studies included, but a course on the order of conventionally fractionated 70 Gy was considered for the purposes of the analysis (with an approximately ≥6-month estimated interval between prior and subsequent treatment in most cases). Factors likely associated with reduced risk of BE include nonconsecutive daily treatment, lower extent of circumferential tumor involvement around the vessel, and no surgical manipulation before or after SBRT. Conclusions Initial data pooling for reirradiation involving the carotid artery resulted in 3 preliminary models compared in this Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic (HyTEC) report. More recent experiences with alternating fractionation schedules and additional risk-reduction strategies are also presented. Complications data for the most critical structures such as spinal cord and carotid artery are so limited that they cannot be viewed as strong conclusions of probability of risk, but rather, as a general guideline for consideration. There is a great need for better reporting standards as noted in the High Dose per Fraction, Hypofractionated Treatment Effects in the Clinic introductory paper.

papers.title: Maximizing Tumor Control and Limiting Complications With Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy for Pancreatic Cancer
papers.abstract: Purpose Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) and stereotactic ablative body radiation therapy is being increasingly used for pancreatic cancer (PCa), particularly in patients with locally advanced and borderline resectable disease. A wide variety of dose fractionation schemes have been reported in the literature. This HyTEC review uses tumor control probability models to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of the various SBRT treatment regimens used in the treatment of patients with localized PCa. Methods and materials A PubMed search was performed to review the published literature on the use of hypofractionated SBRT (usually in 1-5 fractions) for PCa in various clinical scenarios (eg, preoperative [neoadjuvant], borderline resectable, and locally advanced PCa). The linear quadratic model with α/β= 10 Gy was used to address differences in fractionation. Logistic tumor control probability models were generated using maximum likelihood parameter fitting. Results After converting to 3-fraction equivalent doses, the pooled reported data and associated models suggests that 1-year local control (LC) without surgery is ≈79% to 86% after the equivalent of 30 to 36 Gy in 3 fractions, showing a dose response in the range of 25 to 36 Gy, and decreasing to less than 70% 1-year LC at doses below 24 Gy in 3 fractions. The 33 Gy in 5 fraction regimen (Alliance A021501) corresponds to 28.2 Gy in 3 fractions, for which the HyTEC pooled model had 77% 1-year LC without surgery. Above an equivalent dose of 28 Gy in 3 fractions, with margin-negative resection the 1-year LC exceeded 90%. Conclusions Pooled analyses of reported tumor control probabilities for commonly used SBRT dose-fractionation schedules for PCa suggests a dose response. These findings should be viewed with caution given the challenges and limitations of this review. Additional data are needed to better understand the dose or fractionation-response of SBRT for PCa.

papers.title: Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy for Spinal Metastases: Tumor Control Probability Analyses and Recommended Reporting Standards
papers.abstract: Purpose We sought to investigate the tumor control probability (TCP) of spinal metastases treated with stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) in 1 to 5 fractions. Methods and materials PubMed-indexed articles from 1995 to 2018 were eligible for data extraction if they contained SBRT dosimetric details correlated with actuarial 2-year local tumor control rates. Logistic dose-response models of collected data were compared in terms of physical dose and 3-fraction equivalent dose. Results Data were extracted from 24 articles with 2619 spinal metastases. Physical dose TCP modeling of 2-year local tumor control from the single-fraction data were compared with data from 2 to 5 fractions, resulting in an estimated α/β = 6 Gy, and this was used to pool data. Acknowledging the uncertainty intrinsic to the data extraction and modeling process, the 90% TCP corresponded to 20 Gy in 1 fraction, 28 Gy in 2 fractions, 33 Gy in 3 fractions, and (with extrapolation) 40 Gy in 5 fractions. The estimated TCP for common fractionation schemes was 82% at 18 Gy, 90% for 20 Gy, and 96% for 24 Gy in a single fraction, 82% for 24 Gy in 2 fractions, and 78% for 27 Gy in 3 fractions. Conclusions Spinal SBRT with the most common fractionation schemes yields 2-year estimates of local control of 82% to 96%. Given the heterogeneity in the tumor control estimates extracted from the literature, with variability in reporting of dosimetry data and the definition of and statistical methods of reporting tumor control, care should be taken interpreting the resultant model-based estimates. Depending on the clinical intent, the improved TCP with higher dose regimens should be weighed against the potential risks for greater toxicity. We encourage future reports to provide full dosimetric data correlated with tumor local control to allow future efforts of modeling pooled data.

papers.title: Tumor Control Probability of Radiosurgery and Fractionated Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Brain Metastases
papers.abstract: Purpose As part of the American Association of Physicists in Medicine Working Group on Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy, tumor control probability (TCP) after stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and fractionated stereotactic radiosurgery (fSRS) for brain metastases was modeled based on pooled dosimetric and clinical data from published English-language literature. Methods and materials PubMed-indexed studies published between January 1995 and September 2017 were used to evaluate dosimetric and clinical predictors of TCP after SRS or fSRS for brain metastases. Eligible studies had ≥10 patients and included detailed dose-fractionation data with corresponding ≥1-year local control (LC) data, typically evaluated as a >20% increase in diameter of the targeted lesion using the pre-SRS diameter as a reference. Results Of 2951 potentially eligible manuscripts, 56 included sufficient dose-volume data for analyses. Accepting that necrosis and pseudoprogression can complicate the assessment of LC, for tumors ≤20 mm, single-fraction doses of 18 and 24 Gy corresponded with >85% and 95% 1-year LC rates, respectively. For tumors 21 to 30 mm, an 18 Gy single-fraction dose was associated with 75% LC. For tumors 31 to 40 mm, a 15 Gy single-fraction dose yielded ∼69% LC. For 3- to 5-fraction fSRS using doses in the range of 27 to 35 Gy, 80% 1-year LC has been achieved for tumors of 21 to 40 mm in diameter. Conclusions TCP for SRS and fSRS are presented. For small lesions ≤20 mm, single doses of ≈18 Gy appear generally associated with excellent rates of LC; for melanoma, higher doses seem warranted. For larger lesions >20 mm, local control rates appear to be ≈ 70% to 75% with usual doses of 15 to 18 Gy, and in this setting, fSRS regimens should be considered. Greater consistency in reporting of dosimetric and LC data is needed to facilitate future pooled analyses. As systemic and biologic therapies evolve, updated analyses will be needed to further assess the necessity, efficacy, and toxicity of SRS and fSRS.

papers.title: Spinal Cord Dose Tolerance to Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
papers.abstract: Spinal cord tolerance data for stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) were extracted from published reports, reviewed, and modelled. For de novo SBRT delivered in 1 to 5 fractions, the following spinal cord point maximum doses (D max ) are estimated to be associated with a 1% to 5% risk of radiation myelopathy (RM): 12.4 to 14.0 Gy in 1 fraction, 17.0 Gy in 2 fractions, 20.3 Gy in 3 fractions, 23.0 Gy in 4 fractions, and 25.3 Gy in 5 fractions. For reirradiation SBRT delivered in 1 to 5 fractions, reported factors associated with a lower risk of RM include cumulative thecal sac equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions with an alpha/beta of 2 (EQD2 2 ) D max ≤70 Gy; SBRT thecal sac EQD2 2 D max ≤25 Gy, thecal sac SBRT EQD2 2 D max to cumulative EQD2 2 D max ratio ≤0.5, and a minimum time interval to reirradiation of ≥5 months. Larger studies containing complete institutional cohorts with dosimetric data of patients treated with spine SBRT, with and without RM, are required to refine RM risk estimates.
